planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed well into the 70s; Passport ripens earlier than most French Charentais types, making it a good option where the season is too short for classic imported Charentais melons.

directions: Passport is a compact-vined hybrid bred to bring true French Charentais eating quality within reach of gardeners with shorter or cooler summers than the Charentais region of France. Fruit is small and round, about 2-3 pounds, with smooth gray-green skin faintly ribbed at the blossom end and deep orange, intensely aromatic flesh with a very high sugar content. Because Charentais types slip cleanly from the vine only when fully ripe, check daily near the expected harvest window and cut fruit that shows a slight crack or softening at the stem rather than waiting for it to detach on its own. Its shorter vines and earlier maturity make it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting restaurant-quality melon flavor without a long, hot growing season.

common_name: TAM Dew Melon (Texas A&M Downy Mildew-Resistant Honeydew)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past 70°F; bred for the long, hot summers of the southern Great Plains and Gulf Coast, so it needs a full warm season to size up and sweeten properly.

directions: TAM Dew was released by Texas A&M's melon breeding program to give southern growers a honeydew with better resistance to downy mildew than older honeydew varieties, which historically struggled in humid southern conditions. Vines carry smooth, creamy-white rinds around thick, sweet, light green flesh on fruit that typically run 4-6 pounds at harvest. Like other honeydew types it does not slip from the vine, so watch for the rind to shift from a hard green-white to a softer creamy yellow-white and the blossom end to yield slightly to gentle pressure. Give it the full length of a hot summer and consistent moisture through fruit sizing for the best sugar content at harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed into the 70s; its strong disease package suits growers who have had trouble with fusarium wilt or vine decline in previous melon plantings.

directions: Aphrodite is a widely grown commercial Eastern shipper-type cantaloupe bred with resistance to fusarium wilt and tolerance to several common vine and foliar diseases, traits that also make it a dependable performer in home gardens with a history of melon problems. It produces uniform, heavily netted, oval fruit averaging 5-6 pounds with firm, deep orange flesh and a small seed cavity, and vines hold up well and keep setting fruit through extended harvest periods. Ripe fruit develops a full slip, separating cleanly from the vine with light pressure, along with a shift to a more golden background color under the netting and a sweet aroma at the blossom end. Its vigorous, disease-tolerant vines and consistent fruit size make it a good choice for gardeners who want reliable yields without babying a finicky heirloom melon.
